content: Between April 1 and December 31, 2018, a total of 286 index clients agreed to bring their contacts to implementing partner (IP) clinics for HIV testing services (HTS). Trained providers reached and tested 369 contacts of these index clients. Among these contacts, 144 were linked to HIV-positive female sex workers, 109 were linked to HIV-positive men who have sex with men, and 116 were linked to HIV-positive clients of female sex workers. The index testing modalities were implemented across 13 sites, and the client-referral approach was reported to be the most effective across the network. Voluntary Partner Referral (VPR) and Risk Network Referral (RNR) strategies were found to improve case detection among key and priority populations and were deemed acceptable strategies for index testing in these groups. India’s HIV epidemic is concentrated among key populations, including men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, and female sex workers. The National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) implements targeted interventions (TI) for these populations. The LINKAGES project in India, funded by USAID and PEPFAR and led by FHI 360, partnered with NACP to engage individuals from key populations in index testing, including those not reached by the TI program. LINKAGES India adapted index testing to include two approaches: Voluntary Partner Referral (VPR) and Risk Network Referral (RNR). VPR aligns with WHO guidelines and allows people living with HIV (PLHIV) to voluntarily identify spouses, partners, and children at risk for HIV. It offers options for referral, including client-referral, contact-referral, provider-referral, and dual-referral, while ensuring safety and confidentiality. Providers offering VPR assess for intimate partner violence (IPV) and meet minimum requirements to support clients facing such risks. RNR extends beyond VPR by offering PLHIV additional self-guided options to informally link broader social and risk-network members to HIV testing and services through online and coupon-based referrals. These strategies do not require PLHIV to name or know the names of their contacts and allow referrals without disclosing the referral source. Index testing was implemented in both TI and non-TI sites in six high HIV-burden districts in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. Peer navigators facilitated index testing in TI sites, while community mobilizers took on this role in non-TI sites. A standard operating procedure for index testing was developed, and outreach teams were trained on partner notification, risk mitigation, and documentation. Testing was conducted through facility-based and community-based approaches, such as drop-in centers and community events. Challenges in partner identification, notification, referral, and tracking were addressed through counseling and information provision to community members and service providers. Violence redressal committees resolved issues related to fear of disclosure and IPV risks. The case detection rate among spouses was 41%, higher than the 8% rate among other partners. Index testing accounted for 21% of total case detection during the 12-month reporting period. Of the 393 key population individuals diagnosed with HIV through index testing, 302 were linked to treatment by the end of September 2018. Online programs like Talk About Your Business Safely (TABS) and iFlex were developed to scale up HIV services for men who have sex with men and transgender women in Jamaica. These programs, part of the LINKAGES project, are supported by USAID and PEPFAR and led by FHI 360. Local civil society organizations (CSOs) run these programs, employing online outreach workers to engage individuals with HIV-related information and link them to offline services. Outreach workers use standardized messaging and client engagement tactics through passive (social media content) and active (private online conversations) approaches. Between January and December 2018, over 1,400 individuals were engaged in online conversations, with 452 men who have sex with men presenting at physical locations for services. Nearly half (47%) of these individuals received HIV testing. Most online clients were aged 24 years or younger (68%) and were engaged through platforms like Grindr (35%), Instagram (23%), and Facebook (15%). Reasons for declining testing included recent testing (60%), discomfort with testing at the time (15%), or already knowing their positive status (6%). Online social network outreach accounted for 74% of all HIV tests administered. The Eastern Deanery AIDS Relief Program (EDARP) in Nairobi, Kenya, is a Catholic faith-based organization providing integrated HIV and TB prevention, care, and treatment. Founded in 1993, EDARP serves over 1 million people through a linked community-to-facility care model, employing 1,200 community health workers (CHWs) supervised by 410 clinical staff. All activities align with Kenyan Ministry of Health (MoH) guidelines. EDARP focuses on prevention, care, and treatment for the general population, with an emphasis on youth, key populations, and men who have not previously accessed HIV services. CHWs generate demand for HIV testing services (HTS) through outreach, promotion of HIV self-testing, and community mobilization. Partner notification services (PNS) were re-emphasized in June 2019, achieving 100% linkage of HIV-positive patients to care. From July 2018 to June 2019, 119,604 people received facility-based HTS at EDARP clinics, with 1,651 adults and 52 children testing positive. A concentrated effort to target high-risk individuals began in June 2019, including a PNS intervention. Between July and September 2019, 4,368 partners were elicited from HIV-positive clients, with 21% of negative partners placed on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). EDARP also integrated HIV self-testing into its interventions, distributing 2,058 kits. All individuals with reactive results received confirmatory testing.
